extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students studying real analysis (readers of Rudin) and instructors assigning exercises
extracted.subtask_description: A set of numbered real-analysis exercises (with difficulty ratings, hints, and references to Rudin) covering limits, continuity, compactness, connectedness, discontinuities, monotonicity, limits at infinity, and basic differentiation. Intended as practice problems and proofs to accompany textbook material.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.2:7 When can one compose limit-statements?
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate when composition of limit statements is valid; give counterexample showing 'if f(x)→q as x→p and g(y)→r as y→q then g(f(x))→r' can fail. Prove equivalence of two conditions guaranteeing lim_{x→p} g(f(x)) = r when f:E⊆X→Y, g:F⊆Y→Z, lim_{x→p} f(x)=q, q a limit point of F, and lim_{y→q} g(y)=r: (i) either q∈F and g is continuous at q, or (ii) there exists ε>0 such that q ∉ f(N_ε(p)∩E) (i.e., f does not take value q arbitrarily close to p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes explicit counterexample: f(x)=x sin(1/x) for x≠0, f(0)=0 and g(x)=0 for x≠0, g(0)=1 to show lim g(f(x)) can differ. Emphasizes distinct meanings of 'as x→p f(x)→q' (values close to q vs. values unequal to q approaching q).

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.2:8 Two meanings of 'neighborhood' have similar properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare Rudin's 'neighborhood' (open ball) with the topologist's notion (any set with p interior). Show equivalence that a topologist's neighborhood contains a Rudin neighborhood; prove continuity equivalences: f is continuous at p iff inverse images of neighborhoods/topologist's neighborhoods of f(p) contain neighborhoods/topologist's neighborhoods of p; and relate limit-points and sequence limits to topologist's neighborhoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No proofs asked for in last part. Encourages thinking about equivalent formulations using either notion of neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.2:9 At-most-countably-many-to-one continuous maps and perfect sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'at most countably many to one' (preimage f^{-1}(y) is at most countable for every y). If f:X→Y is continuous and at most countably many-to-one between metric spaces, and E⊆X is compact perfect, show f(E) is a perfect subset of Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: parallels behavior of continuous maps on compact and connected sets; may be assigned with adjacent sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.2:10 k-dimensional space-filling curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming existence of continuous surjection Φ:[0,1]→[0,1]^2 with Φ=(a,b), use compositions to build continuous surjections [0,1]→[0,1]^n for all n≥2 and an 'infinite-dimensional' space-filling curve: (a) show a 3-D onto map can be formed via (a(t),a(b(t)),b(b(t))); (b) generalize to n-dimensions using iterated composites b^i; (c) deduce for any sequence (x_n) in [0,1] there exists t with a(b^{n-1}(t))=x_n for all n, using compactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains notation b^0(t)=t; hint for (c): for each N the set of t satisfying first N equations is nonempty, then use compactness. Remarks mention Rudin notation and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.2:11 Plane-filling curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Using Rudin's map [0,1]→[0,1]^2, deduce existence of a continuous map R→R^2 by mapping [n,n+1] onto larger and larger squares and gluing intervals appropriately; note generalization to R→R^k for all k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: part (c) of 4.2:10 used compactness of [0,1] so R is different; leads into next exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.2:12 No infinite-dimensional analog
rubrics_metrics.description: Show there does not exist a sequence of continuous functions f_n:R→R such that for every sequence (x_n) in R there is t∈R with f_n(t)=x_n for all n. Hint suggests choosing x1 large enough to rule out solutions in small intervals iteratively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive hint: choose x1 large so no t∈[-1,1] satisfies f1(t)=x1, then choose x2 large so no t∈[-2,2] satisfies f2(t)=x2, etc., to derive contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.2:13 Results for R imply same for [0,1)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Exhibit continuous surjections R→[0,1) and [0,1)→R; (b) deduce from (a) and 4.2:11 a continuous function [0,1)→[0,1)^2; (c) deduce there does not exist infinite sequence of continuous g_n:[0,1)→[0,1) with universal interpolation property analogous to 4.2:12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relies on part (a) and previous exercises; references dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.2:14 Sequence of continuous functions equivalent to one function into sequence-space
rubrics_metrics.description: Show relationship between sequences of [0,1]-valued continuous functions f_i:X→[0,1] and a single continuous map f:X→[0,1]^J (space of sequences) with metric d((x_i),(y_i))=Σ |x_i-y_i|/2^i: equivalence of continuity of each f_i and continuity of f. Extend to R^J by replacing term with min(|x_i-y_i|,2^{-i}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (a) show d is a metric; (b) continuity equivalence; (c) explain why naive formula fails on R^J and give corrected metric. Useful to view infinite product topology metrically.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.2:15 Set where two continuous functions agree is closed
rubrics_metrics.description: If f,g:X→Y are continuous, show E={x∈X|f(x)=g(x)} is closed. (b) Show (a) implies result of earlier 4:R3. (c) Deduce main result of 4:R4 about equality at point p implies equality on neighborhood under stated conditions. (d) Converse: for any closed E in metric space X there exist continuous f,g:X→Y with equality set E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple proofs possible: direct closed-set verification, showing complement open, or using continuity of x↦d(f(x),g(x)) and noting E is its zero-set. Dependencies to other exercises noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.2:16 Functions which approach a limit everywhere
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:X→Y is (not assumed continuous) and lim_{x→p} f(x) exists for every p∈X, define g(p)=lim_{x→p} f(x). Show g is continuous. Remarks: can weaken hypothesis to limit existing at non-isolated points and define appropriately at isolated points; also can assume f defined on dense subset E and still define g on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points out strengthening and weakenings; suggests handling isolated points and dense-domain cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.3:0 True/False questions on continuity and compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of True/False statements about continuous functions on compact spaces, boundedness, supremum attainment, and uniform continuity of 1/x on various domains, with answers provided (g)F, (d)F, (b)T, (c)F, (e)T, (a)T, (f)F, (i)T, (h)F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements include: a) function on compact space equivalence with graph compactness; b) etc.; intended to check understanding of compactness and uniform continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.3:1 On what metric spaces is every function continuous / uniformly continuous?
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Characterize metric spaces X such that every function X→Y (to any metric space Y) is continuous. (b) Characterize X such that every function X→Y is uniformly continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic exercises — expect discrete/indiscrete and finite cases; difficulty rated d:3.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.3:2 Continuous periodic functions on R are uniformly continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If f:R→X continuous and periodic with period c>0, then f is uniformly continuous. (b) Show sin(x^2) is not uniformly continuous (though sin x is).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periodicity to reduce to compact interval; for (b) observe rapidly varying argument causes failure of uniform continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.3:3 Continuous map on R^k takes bounded sets to bounded sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:R^k→X is continuous and E⊆R^k bounded, show f(E) is bounded in X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Heine-Borel or preimage of boundedness via continuity; rated d:2.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.3:4 A shrinking map on a compact space has a fixed point
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If K compact and f:K→K satisfies d(f(x),f(y))<d(x,y) for all distinct x,y, show unique fixed point exists. (b) Give counterexample if '<' weakened to '≤'. (c) Show false if K noncompact [0,1), [0,∞), or R. (d) Deduce impossibility of continuous f:K→K with d(f(x),f(y))>d(x,y) for all distinct x,y. (e) Show lim_{n→∞} f^n(x)=p for all x. (f) Generalize for g:K→X surjective-on-K with d(g(x),g(y))>d(x,y) to conclude unique fixed point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main part (a) essential; remaining parts illustrate boundaries of the theorem and relate to other exercises (see 4.3:8).

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.3:5 Uniform 'either/or' continuity of two or more functions
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For compact X and functions f:X→Y, g:X→Z such that at each p at least one of f,g is continuous, show: for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 s.t. d(p,q)<δ implies either d(f(p),f(q))<ε or d(g(p),g(q))<ε. (b) Ask whether analogous result holds for infinite families f_i and ε_i: can one find a single δ valid for all i?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (b) invites counterexample or further conditions; note compactness and finiteness matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.3:6 Weak condition implying boundedness
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If E⊆K where K compact and f:E→Y (not assumed continuous) satisfies: for some ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that whenever d_X(p,q)<δ one has d_Y(f(p),f(q))<ε, then f must be bounded. (b) Deduce Rudin 4:R8 from (a). (c) Find bounded noncompact X and uniformly continuous f:X→Y such that f(X) is not bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an open cover argument in (a); (c) shows uniform continuity need not imply image boundedness without compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.3:7 More on functions which approach a limit everywhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f:X→Y such that lim_{x→p} f(x) exists for every p and D⊆X is set of discontinuities of f, show for any compact K⊆X the set D∩K is countable. Suggestion: define w(p)=lim_{ε→0} diam(f(N_ε(p))) and argue finiteness for levels >1/n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refines 4.2:16; uses compactness and diameter-based counting argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.3:8 Weakly shrinking maps on compact spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If K compact and f:K→K satisfies d(f(x),f(y))≤d(x,y) for all x,y, show f is surjective iff d(f(x),f(y))=d(x,y) for all x,y. (b) Deduce: if K compact and g:K→K continuous with d(g(x),g(y))≥d(x,y) for all x,y then d(g(x),g(y))=d(x,y) for all x,y (hence not strictly expanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare with 4.3:4; use compactness and surjectivity properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.4:0 True/False on continuity and connectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Two statements: (a) Every continuous map R→Q is constant. (b) Every continuous map Q→R is constant. Answers given elsewhere; exercise references 4.2:3 as relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to test understanding of connectedness and density of Q vs R.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.4:1 No continuous one-to-one map from circle to line
rubrics_metrics.description: Let S be unit circle in R^2. Show there is no continuous one-to-one function S→R. You may use parameterizations and equivalent characterizations of S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use topological properties: removing a point from circle leaves connectedness different than line; rated d:2.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.4:2 Closed half-line not like whole line
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Prove no one-to-one continuous map [0,∞)→R. (b) Prove no one-to-one continuous map R→[0,∞). (c) Deduce corresponding results for [0,1) in place of [0,∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise contrasts topological differences despite some similarities between [0,1) and R demonstrated earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.4:3 A space-filling curve cannot be one-to-one
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For n>1 and p∈[0,1]^n show removing p leaves the set connected? (b) Show existence of one-to-one continuous map [0,1]→[0,1]^n leads to contradiction with known facts about continuous bijections between compact metric spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: compare connectedness properties of domain and codomain after removing a point; relates to earlier space-filling curve constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.4:4 Continuous functions on disconnected sets
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Characterize disconnected metric spaces X as unions of pairwise disjoint nonempty open-and-closed sets Ei with |I|>1. (b) If X is such union and f:X→Y has restrictions f|_{Ei} continuous for each i, show f is continuous. (c) Conversely, if every f whose restrictions are continuous is continuous, show each Ei must be open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses basic connectedness topological characterizations; suggestions to think first about two-element case.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.5:0 True/False about discontinuities
rubrics_metrics.description: Four T/F questions: (a) f(x)=1/x has discontinuity of second kind at 0. (b) f(x)=1/x for x≠0, f(0)=0 has discontinuity of second kind at 0. (c) If f continuous at 0 and g(0) exists? (statement paraphrased) (d) Construction question about building f from g with certain properties. Answers provided earlier in document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates to Rudin exercises R16–R18 and classification of discontinuities.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.6:0 True/False on monotonic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Every constant function R→R is both monotonically increasing and decreasing. (b) For any function f:R→R, the set {x|f is discontinuous at x} is closed. Answers given: (b)T, (a)F in this chunk's answer section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests edge cases and correct definitions for monotonicity and discontinuity sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.6:1 Increasing function local control
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose α:[a,b]→R is monotonically increasing. Show: for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that whenever a≤x<y≤b and y−x<δ, either α(y)−α(x)<ε or there exists z∈[x,y] s.t. α(z+)-α(z−)≥ε and (α(y)−α(z+))+(α(z−)−α(x))<ε; with endpoint conventions for z=a or z=b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures that increasing functions change slowly except for jump discontinuities; rated d:?? (text indicates complexity).

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.7:0 True/False on infinite limits and limits at infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Collection of T/F statements and answers about limits at infinity, behavior of continuous functions on bounded segments, sequences f(n) convergence implying limit at infinity, and sum of functions with +∞ and -∞ limits. Answers provided: (d)F, (b)T, (e)F, (c)T, (a)F, (f)F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforces understanding of limits at infinity and Cauchy-like criteria for function limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.7:1 Function on R with limits at ±∞ is uniformly continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:R→R continuous and lim_{x→+∞} f(x) and lim_{x→−∞} f(x) both exist (as real numbers), then f is uniformly continuous on R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses extending uniform continuity on tails and compactness on central interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.7:2 Continuous map asymptotic to uniformly continuous map
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Strengthen Theorem 4.19: for continuous f:X→Y and compact K⊆X, for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that for all p∈K and x∈X with d(p,x)<δ one has d(f(p),f(x))<ε. (b) Define 'asymptotic' for maps f,g:X→Y meaning for every ε>0 the set {x:d(f(x),g(x))≥ε} is contained in a compact subset. Show continuous map asymptotic to a uniformly continuous map is uniformly continuous, and deduce 4.7:1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives notion of asymptotic closeness outside compact sets and how uniform continuity transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4.7:3 Cauchy criteria for limits of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For complex-valued f on neighborhood of (c,+∞), lim_{x→+∞} f(x) exists iff for every ε>0 there exists M such that |f(x)-f(y)|<ε for all x,y>M. (b) State analogous Cauchy criterion for limit at finite limit point p in metric space. (c) Give examples showing failure if 'complex-valued' is replaced by 'function into metric space Y'; ask for which Y the results hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (c) asks to identify metric spaces where Cauchy criterion holds for function limits — e.g., complete spaces vs others; rated d:2.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5.1:0 True/False on differentiability basics
rubrics_metrics.description: Four T/F items: (a) If a bounded function R→R is continuous then derivative exists everywhere (b) if f differentiable on [0,2] and lim_{t→1} f(t)=7 then f(1)=7 (c) if f,g differentiable then f+g differentiable (d) if f and f+g differentiable then g differentiable. Answers appear in document (b)F, (c)T, (a)T? (context shows answers later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests understanding of derivative existence, continuity implications and linearity of differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5.2:0 True/False on mean value theorem and derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) f(x,y)=x^2−y^2 on R^2 has local extremum at (0,0) ? (b) If f:R→R differentiable and f'(x)=0 then classification? (c) If f everywhere differentiable and f'(n)=1 for infinitely many n then consequences? (paraphrased; see original for precise statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short true/false checks to accompany mean value theorem material and related concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5.2:1 Which differentiable functions are strictly increasing?
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If f continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) with f'(x)≥0 for all x and f'(x)>0 for some x, show f(b)>f(a). (b) For continuous f on interval [a,b] differentiable on (a,b), f is strictly increasing iff (i) f'(x)≥0 for all x∈(a,b), and (ii) for every p<q in (a,b) there is r∈(p,q) with f'(r)>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects derivative sign information to monotonicity; uses mean value theorem and related techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5.2:2 A fake counterexample to Theorem 5.9
rubrics_metrics.description: Discusses subtlety about ratio of velocity components in parametric curves: given parametrized curve (f(t),g(t)), Theorem 5.9's conclusion about equality of ratio of velocity components vs total displacement can be apparently violated; exercise asks to analyze such fake counterexample and reconcile with theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages drawing picture and thinking about directions of velocity vs displacement; rated d:1.
